summary: Defines a human-readable string form for LDAP search filters, which travel on the wire in a binary form. The string form suits LDAP URLs and other applications. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: LDAP clients ask a directory server for entries by sending a filter, and the filter normally travels in a binary form. This document defines the readable text form of that filter, including how to write characters that would otherwise be read as syntax.

subtitle: How to write an LDAP search filter as readable text, such as (&(objectClass=Person)(sn=Jensen)).

tldr.problem: An LDAP search filter travels over the network in a binary form that is not convenient to write by hand, yet people and tools need a readable way to express the same filter.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a string form of the full range of LDAP version 3 search filters, written in prefix notation with parentheses, and an escaping rule that writes special characters as a backslash and two hexadecimal digits.
tldr.outcome: LDAP URLs and other applications can carry a filter that a person can read and edit. The document replaces RFC 2254 and is part of the LDAP technical specification.

facts.label: Characters that must be escaped
facts.value: Asterisk, both parentheses, backslash and NUL

facts.label: Escape form
facts.value: A backslash followed by two hexadecimal digits

facts.label: Input tolerance
facts.value: Implementations should accept strings that are not valid UTF-8

today: RFC 4515 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006. It replaced RFC 2254 and has not been obsoleted since. It is part of the LDAP technical specification and defines the readable string form that LDAP URLs and other applications use.

sections.title: Why a String Form of Filters
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, RFC 4510, defines a network representation of a search filter transmitted to an LDAP server. Some applications find it useful to have a common way of representing these search filters in a human-readable form; LDAP URLs, RFC 4516, are one such application.

This document defines a human-readable string format for representing the full range of possible LDAP version 3 search filters, including extended match filters. It is an integral part of the LDAP technical specification, and it replaces RFC 2254, with the changes summarized in Appendix A.
sections.plainLanguage: The filter a person writes in a search box and the filter that goes over the network are two forms of the same thing. This document defines the readable one, so that the same filter can be typed, stored in a URL, or handed to another program.

sections.title: The Binary Filter Being Represented
sections.content:
An LDAP search filter is defined in Section 4.5.1 of RFC 4511 as a choice between ten alternatives: and, or and not, which combine other filters; equalityMatch, substrings, greaterOrEqual and lessOrEqual, which compare an attribute with a value; present, which asks whether an attribute exists at all; approxMatch, which asks for an approximate match; and extensibleMatch, which names a matching rule and may include the distinguished name in the comparison.

A substring filter names an attribute and a sequence of pieces: an initial value, any number of any values, and a final value, where the initial and the final can occur at most once. An equality, ordering or approximate comparison is an AttributeValueAssertion, which pairs an attribute description with an assertion value. A MatchingRuleAssertion carries an optional matching rule identifier, an optional attribute description, the value to match, and a flag saying whether the attributes of the distinguished name count as part of the entry.

The AttributeDescription is the string representation of the attribute description discussed in RFC 4512. The AttributeValue and AssertionValue octet strings have the form defined in RFC 4517, and the filter is encoded for transmission using the Basic Encoding Rules of ASN.1, with the simplifications described in RFC 4511.
sections.plainLanguage: On the wire, a filter is one of ten kinds of thing: a combination of other filters, a comparison, a substring, a presence test, an approximate match, or a match with a named rule. The string form has to be able to say all of them.

sections.title: The String Grammar
sections.content:
The string representation of an LDAP search filter is a string of UTF-8 encoded Unicode characters, defined by a grammar written in the ABNF notation of RFC 4234. The format uses prefix notation: a filter is a left parenthesis, a filter component and a right parenthesis. A filter component is either a combination of filters or a single item, where a combination is an ampersand for 'and', a vertical bar for 'or', and an exclamation mark for 'not'.

An item is a simple match, a presence test, a substring match or an extensible match. A simple match is an attribute, a filter type and an assertion value. The filter types are equality, approximate match using a tilde and equals sign, greater than or equal using a right angle bracket and equals sign, and less than or equal using a left angle bracket and equals sign.

A presence test is an attribute followed by an equals sign and an asterisk. A substring match is an attribute, an equals sign, an optional initial value, any number of any values written as asterisks, and an optional final value. An extensible match is written either as an attribute, optionally followed by the ':dn' marker and optionally followed by a matching rule, then a colon and an equals sign and the value; or as the ':dn' marker and a matching rule, then a colon and an equals sign and the value, with the attribute left out. The RFC notes that although both the substring and presence productions can produce the 'attr=*' construct, that construct is used only to denote a presence filter.
sections.plainLanguage: Filters are written with parentheses and prefix operators: an ampersand means all of these, a vertical bar means any of these, and an exclamation mark means not. Inside, an attribute is compared to a value, to a piece of a value with asterisks, or to nothing at all.

sections.title: Escaping Special Characters
sections.content:
The valueencoding rule ensures that the entire filter string is a valid UTF-8 string, and provides that the octets representing the ASCII characters for asterisk, left parenthesis, right parenthesis, backslash and NUL are represented as a backslash followed by the two hexadecimal digits representing the value of the encoded octet. This simple escaping mechanism eliminates filter-parsing ambiguities and allows any filter that can be represented in LDAP to be represented as a NUL-terminated string. Other octets that are part of the normal set may be escaped this way too, for example non-printing ASCII characters.

For assertion values that contain UTF-8 character data, each octet of the character to be escaped is replaced by a backslash and two hex digits, which form a single octet in the code of the character. The RFC's example is a filter checking whether the 'cn' attribute contained the character '*' anywhere in it, which is written as (cn=*\2a*).

Implementations MUST escape all octets greater than 0x7F that are not part of a valid UTF-8 encoding sequence when they generate a string representation of a search filter. Implementations SHOULD accept as input strings that are not valid UTF-8 strings, which the RFC says is necessary because RFC 2254 did not clearly define the term 'string representation', and in particular did not mention that the string representation of an LDAP search filter is a string of UTF-8 encoded Unicode characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Five characters carry meaning inside a filter, so they are written as a backslash and two hexadecimal digits when they are part of a value. The same trick lets any binary value, including NUL bytes, be written down.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives these filters as examples of the ordinary notation: (cn=Babs Jensen), (!(cn=Tim Howes)), (&(objectClass=Person)(|(sn=Jensen)(cn=Babs J*))), (o=univ*of*mich*) and (seeAlso=).

The extensible matching examples are (cn:caseExactMatch:=Fred Flintstone), which uses the matching rule 'caseExactMatch'; (cn:=Betty Rubble), which uses a MatchingRuleAssertion form with no matching rule; (sn:dn:2.4.6.8.10:=Barney Rubble), where the ':oid' notation names the matching rule identified by the object identifier 2.4.6.8.10 and ':dn' says the attributes of an entry's distinguished name should be considered part of the entry when the match is evaluated; (o:dn:=Ace Industry), an equality match except that DN components count as part of the entry; (:1.2.3:=Wilma Flintstone), a filter to apply to any attribute supporting the matching rule given, since the attribute has been left out; and (:DN:2.4.6.8.10:=Dino), also applied to any attribute supporting the matching rule, with attributes in the DN also considered.

The escaping examples are (o=Parens R Us \28for all your parenthetical needs\29), (cn=*\2A*), (filename=C:\5cMyFile), (bin=\00\00\00\04), (sn=Lu\c4\8di\c4\87) and (1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.0=\04\02\48\69). The first shows the escaping of parenthesis characters, the second shows a '*' written so it is not read as a substring indicator, the third escapes the backslash itself, the fourth searches for the four-octet value 00 00 00 04, the fifth shows various non-ASCII UTF-8 characters, and the last demonstrates the assertion of a BER-encoded value.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples cover the plain cases, the extended match syntax where a named matching rule is used, and the escape sequences. An asterisk in a value has to be escaped, or it is read as a wildcard.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the string representation itself has no known security implications, but LDAP search filters do: they are interpreted by LDAP servers to select entries from which data is retrieved. LDAP servers should take care to protect the data they maintain from unauthorized access, and the RFC refers the reader to the Security Considerations sections of RFC 4511 and RFC 4513 for more information.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing a filter down is not itself dangerous. Deciding who may read the entries a filter selects is the server's job, and that is covered elsewhere.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2254
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the changes. The ISO 10646 reference was replaced with a Unicode reference, and the document now states that the string representation is a string of UTF-8 encoded Unicode characters. All of the ABNF was revised to use the common productions from RFC 4512, and the 'value' rule was replaced with a new 'assertionvalue' rule inside the simple, extensible and substring rules, matching a change made in RFC 4517. Parentheses were added around the components of the extensible subproductions for clarity, and the attr, matchingrule and assertionvalue rules were revised to reference the productions in RFC 4512 and RFC 4511 more precisely. The names 'greater' and 'less' were replaced with 'greaterorequal' and 'lessorequal' to avoid confusion, and the valueencoding rule with its normal and escaped rules was introduced to reduce the dependence on descriptive text.

The editorial changes include renaming the document title to carry the 'LDAP:' prefix, correcting the LDAP search filter ABNF so it matches RFC 4511, and adding several examples, including (seeAlso=), (cn:=Betty Rubble), (:1.2.3:=Wilma Flintstone) and (1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.0=\04\02\48\69).
sections.plainLanguage: The wording and the examples were tidied up, the grammar was rewritten with the shared productions from the newer LDAP documents, and the document now says plainly that the string form is UTF-8.

viz.caption: The string grammar as given in RFC 4515

data.title: Filter string grammar
data.code:
filter         = LPAREN filtercomp RPAREN
filtercomp     = and / or / not / item
and            = AMPERSAND filterlist
or             = VERTBAR filterlist
not            = EXCLAMATION filter
filterlist     = 1*filter
item           = simple / present / substring / extensible
simple         = attr filtertype assertionvalue
filtertype     = equal / approx / greaterorequal / lessorequal
extensible     = ( attr [dnattrs] [matchingrule] COLON EQUALS assertionvalue )
                / ( [dnattrs] matchingrule COLON EQUALS assertionvalue )
present        = attr EQUALS ASTERISK
substring      = attr EQUALS [initial] any [final]

viz.caption: The pieces a filter is built from

items.title: attr=value
items.text: An exact match on one attribute.

items.title: attr=*
items.text: The attribute is present. The asterisk is a wildcard only in a substring.

items.title: attr:rule:=value
items.text: A match using a named matching rule, optionally with :dn to include the distinguished name.

viz.caption: Examples of the escaping mechanism from RFC 4515

data.title: Escaped filters
data.code:
(o=Parens R Us \28for all your parenthetical needs\29)
(cn=*\2A*)
(filename=C:\5cMyFile)
(bin=\00\00\00\04)
(sn=Lu\c4\8di\c4\87)
